The Cape skink (Trachylepis capensis) exhibits a maximum reproductive output of twelve young per litter [N_R_i = twelve young per litter] produced during a single annual litter [F_R_i = single annual litter], a pattern consistent with other southern African members of the Trachylepis genus. Neonates emerge from the incubating egg at a wet weight of one gram [Wwb = one gram], a value comparable to that observed in the congeneric Chalcides chalcides. This modest birth mass is typical of small-bodied scincids and reflects the relatively low maternal investment per offspring that characterizes species producing moderately large litters. The timing of these developmental events is tightly linked to thermal conditions, and available data indicate that the key reproductive and developmental milestones reported here were measured at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the embryonic development period culminates in hatching after approximately ninety days [ab = approximately ninety days], a duration that falls within the expected range for a species of this body size and geographic distribution. This protracted incubation period is likely tied to the relatively low metabolic heat production of the parchment-shelled eggs, which rely entirely on environmental warmth for their development. Following emergence, the neonate, weighing one gram [Wwb = one gram], embarks on a rapid growth trajectory. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult individuals has been recorded at 57.92 grams [Wwi = 57.92 grams], a substantial increase that represents a nearly sixty-fold gain from the birth mass. This adult body size places Trachylepis capensis among the medium-sized members of its genus in the region.

Female Cape skinks reach sexual maturation at a comparatively advanced age relative to their lifespan. Specifically, the time from hatching to the onset of puberty in females is approximately one year following metamorphosis [tp = approximately one year following metamorphosis], a delay that likely reflects the time required to accumulate the necessary body condition and fat reserves for success at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]ful reproduction. Data from captive colonies, maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], confirm that the age at birth is 90 days [ab = 90 days], and that the time to pubertal onset is one year (365 days following metamorphosis) [tp = 365 days following metamorphosis]. This relatively late maturation is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth before diverting resources to reproductive effort.

The maximum lifespan of the Cape skink, based on comparisons with the closely related Chalcides chalcides, is estimated at approximately four years [am = approximately four years] under stable thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This longevity is moderate for a reptile of its adult mass of 57.92 grams [Wwi = 57.92 grams], which suggests a relatively slow pace of life with a correspondingly low annual reproductive rate. Indeed, the species' annual output of one litter per season [F_R_i = one litter per season], containing twelve young [N_R_i = containing twelve young] represents a deliberate, low-frequency strategy. The four-year lifespan (4 years) [am = 4 years] further constrains the total lifetime reproductive potential, meaning each female has only a limited number of breeding opportunities at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

Basal metabolic rate measurements for Trachylepis capensis were obtained through respirometry trials conducted at a cooler ambient temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Under these conditions, the standard oxygen consumption was recorded at 0.0031 milliliters per minute [JOi = 0.0031 milliliters per minute], a value that reflects the reduced metabolic demands of a small ectotherm at a sub-optimal thermal state at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This low metabolic rate is consistent with the skink's relatively sedentary foraging mode and its pattern of infrequent reproduction, with each female producing a single annual litter of twelve young [Ri = each female producing a single annual litter of twelve young] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The disparity between the measurement temperature and the preferred thermal range for activity explains the depressed metabolic rate observed in the experiment.
